title: Roadmap
text:
This roadmap breaks the project into sequential milestones with explicit deliverables and acceptance criteria. Status values: not started, in progress, complete.
Cross-cutting concerns (reproducibility, data governance, documentation) apply to every milestone.
A guiding assumption throughout: health is a dynamic, nonstationary quantity. Distributions drift, relationships between variables change over time, and shocks (epidemics, policy changes, demographic transition) create regime shifts. Every milestone therefore treats “the state of health” as a trajectory to be tracked — never a fixed snapshot — and results are always tied to the time window in which they hold.



Goal: Establish the repository, documentation site, and contribution workflow so all later work has a place to live.
Deliverables:

Acceptance criteria:

quarto render builds the site without errors.
A push to main publishes the site automatically.
New contributors can find the project overview, roadmap, and the four Diátaxis entry points from the landing page.

Goal: Produce a provisional, versioned definition of health and of the “state of health” in BC that can be operationalised as measurable indicators, together with the measurement framework that turns it into candidate indicators. The definition is expected to evolve as the project learns what is measurable; revisions are recorded, never silent.
Deliverables:

A definition document covering: conceptual basis (WHO, ICF, capability-based views), the domains, what is deliberately excluded, and a stated revision process.
Proxy discipline: the definition distinguishes the construct (the state of health) from proxies (every indicator), so that no proxy is confused for the state of health, no proxy is taken to define its domain, and composite indices are treated as models rather than measurements.
Temporal semantics in the definition: health is specified as a time-varying state (a trajectory with levels, slopes, and possible discontinuities), not a timeless attribute. The definition states what changes over what timescale, and that indicators are re-evaluated as the underlying population changes.
All resolutions: the definition commits to using all available levels of resolution (individual, neighbourhood/HSDA/LHA, health authority, provincial, external/non-BC), recording the resolution of every datum and result, and treating any fusion across resolutions as a model output with stated assumptions.
A measurement framework: domains and candidate indicator families for each domain (mortality, physical morbidity, mental health, functional status, subjective wellbeing, social wellbeing), each with candidate sources and stated expected temporal behaviour (gradually trending, seasonally varying, shock-prone, or plausibly stable over the analysis window).
Glossary of terms used consistently across the project.

Acceptance criteria:

The definition document is published in the Explanation section of the docs and survives review by at least one domain reviewer.
Every proposed domain maps to at least one candidate indicator with a named, obtainable data source.
The definition explicitly answers: is the state of health a snapshot, a trajectory, or both — and how the project will detect when its own description of health has gone stale.
The definition distinguishes constructs from proxies, and states how results at different resolutions are recorded and combined.
The definition carries a version number and a revision process.

Status: in progress — v0.1 drafted (definition document, measurement framework, glossary); fusing across resolutions and domain additions still to be stress-tested once M2 lands Depends on: M0




Goal: Inventory and characterise the data that describe the state of health in BC over time and space. “Data” is construed broadly: anything publicly available that can be appropriately used to advance the project’s goals — from survey and administrative microdata through published summary statistics.
Deliverables:

Data source catalogue (in the Reference section): coverage period, geography, frequency, licence, access route, refresh cadence, quality notes. Each entry records its form — microdata, indicator table, dashboard, or report figure — since a published summary statistic is as admissible as a raw dataset.
Catalogue entries for external drivers as well: sources outside BC that bear on BC’s health (interprovincial and international patient flows, migration, national/provincial economic conditions, supply chains, cross-border environmental conditions), each tagged with its geographic origin and the mechanism by which it reaches BC.
Acquisition pipeline: scripts that fetch/ingest each source into a reproducible local layout.
Data quality report: known gaps, revisions, suppressions, and definitional breaks.

Acceptance criteria:

Every indicator named in the M1 measurement framework has at least one catalogue entry.
A clean checkout plus the documented commands reproduces the ingested dataset.
The catalogue is judged by “best use of all publicly available information that can be appropriately used” — not “microdata or nothing”: an indicator backed only by published summary statistics still qualifies when it passes licence and governance checks.

Status: in progress — catalogue of 28 sources (all URLs verified), including determinant/stratifier sources and microdata access routes; a Python acquisition pipeline and a data-quality register are drafted. Outstanding: microdata approvals, neighbourhood-level outcomes, and cross-border patient-flow / supply-chain external drivers Depends on: M1




Goal: Describe the state of health in BC over time and space.
Deliverables:

Reproducible analysis pipeline producing trend and map views for each indicator.
Trajectory analysis as the default view: change over time (slopes, turning points, change-point detection) is reported alongside levels; cross-sectional snapshots are treated as slices of the trajectory, not the headline result.
Regime-aware reporting: identified discontinuities (e.g. pandemic years, coding definition changes, health system reforms) are marked on every series, with within-regime and across-regime comparisons kept separate.
A published “State of health in BC” descriptive report (trends, inequalities across health authorities/regions, demographic breakdowns), versioned with its observation window.
Indicator reference pages with definitions, source, and caveats.

Acceptance criteria:

The report regenerates end-to-end from raw data with one documented command.
Each indicator page states its provenance and known limitations.
Every indicator’s page states whether the series is stationary over the covered window; nonstationary series carry their trend/regime interpretation, not a single summary value.

Status: in progress — the pipeline builds and publishes indicators from catalogued Statistics Canada tables, each with regenerable charts and formal regime dating: piecewise-linear segmentation with BIC selection, a residual-permutation break test, and a Kendall-tau trend test, so every series — including the sex breakdowns — is labelled stationary or not over its observed window. The mortality indicator (13-10-0710-01) carries crude and age-standardised (WHO standard) series; life expectancy at birth (13-10-0837-01) carries annual levels by sex; a survey family (13-10-0905-01, ten series across morbidity, mental health, subjective and social wellbeing, and access to care) widens the report beyond mortality; and a sub-provincial view (13-10-0931-01) reports the age-standardised premature-mortality gap across BC’s five health authorities and 17 health service delivery areas. The mortality indicator is also decomposed by five-year age group, each with its own trend and regime summary. Edition 0.3 of the descriptive report (“State of health in BC”) is published and regenerates end-to-end from the published datasets. Outstanding: sub-provincial views for the survey and life-expectancy indicators, and regime-aware within-versus-across-regime comparisons. Depends on: M2




Goal: Characterise which variables are statistically dependent with health outcomes in BC.
Deliverables:

Analysis of association between candidate variables (social, economic, environmental, health-system, behavioural) and health indicators.
Stability analysis before pooling. For every headline association, estimates across subperiods/rolling windows; a single pooled estimate is reported only when the relationship is supported as stable over the analysis window — otherwise time-varying estimates are the result.
Documented methods: variable selection, handling of collinearity, spatial and temporal confounding, stationarity/stability checks, uncertainty reporting.
Results published with effect sizes, caveats, and their estimation window — not just significance flags.

Acceptance criteria:

Methods are documented in the Reference Section; results are explained in plain language in the Explanation section.
Analyses are reproducible from the M2 pipeline.
Every reported association states the time window it was estimated on and whether the relationship was found stable within that window.

Status: not started Depends on: M3




Goal: Characterise the causal structures that produce changes in the state of health.
Deliverables:

Explicit causal diagrams (DAGs) with stated assumptions for key questions.
Dynamic causal structures: time-indexed diagrams capturing lagged effects, feedback loops (e.g. health → economic participation → resources → health), and time-varying confounding; composition changes (mortality selection, migration) are represented where they matter.
Analyses using appropriate designs (longitudinal, quasi-experimental, natural experiments where available).
An assumptions register: what is assumed, why, and what would refute it — including explicit stationarity assumptions (which causal links are assumed stable over the analysis window, and what observed change would invalidate that assumption).

Acceptance criteria:

Each causal claim links to its DAG, data, and assumptions.
Sensitivity analyses quantify how strong unmeasured confounding would need to be to change conclusions.
Each causal claim carries a stated validity window and the monitoring signal that would indicate drift invalidating it.

Status: not started Depends on: M4




Goal: Recommend actions that would improve the cumulative state of health (maximising the time-integrated state of health over time, rather than point-in-time snapshots), with explicit evidence grading and uncertainty.
Deliverables:

Recommendation framework: evidence strength, expected magnitude, feasibility, equity impact, and uncertainty for each recommendation.
Validity conditions: for each recommendation, the M4/M5 findings it rests on, the time window of those findings, and the drift indicators that trigger re-evaluation.
A reviewed set of prioritised recommendations.
A scheduled revision cycle: re-run the pipeline on refreshed data and re-confirm, revise, or withdraw each recommendation.

Acceptance criteria:

Every recommendation traces back to M4/M5 results and its underlying data sources.
Recommendations are published with their confidence level and the conditions under which they should be revisited.
No recommendation is presented as permanently valid; each carries a date and the next scheduled review.

Status: not started Depends on: M4, M5




These run alongside every milestone:

Reproducibility. Every published number regenerates from raw data via documented commands; environments are pinned.
Nonstationarity vigilance. Results are versioned with their observation window; the pipeline is re-run on refreshed data so drift in distributions or relationships is detected rather than assumed away; regime shifts (epidemics, policy changes, coding revisions) are marked as first-class events in every series.
Data governance and ethics. Respect licences, privacy obligations, and Indigenous data sovereignty principles (e.g. OCAP® (First Nations Information Governance Centre, n.d.) and First Nations data governance contexts in BC). No individual-level data in the repository.
Documentation. New capabilities land with matching documentation in the correct Diátaxis section.
Engineering conventions. The top-level framework and interface are written in Python; Python may glue around other tools and languages (including R) where that has a distinct benefit; performance-critical new functionality is implemented in Rust, C, and/or C++ — preferring Rust for greenfield code, and allowing C/C++ to interface with existing low-level libraries. See How to contribute.
Citations. Factual claims about the world are cited: sources are recorded in references.bib and cited inline with Pandoc citation syntax ([@key]), so each page renders its own reference list from the works it cites.
Scope control. The object of study is BC’s health — not exclusively BC-origin data. Explanatory data that bears on BC health but originates elsewhere (interprovincial and international patient flows, migration, supply chains, economic or environmental disturbances from outside the province) is in scope; what is “BC only” is the outcome being explained. Expansion of the object of study beyond BC is out of scope until the BC analysis is mature (see README).

title: Health is not stationary
text: This page frames an assumption that runs through the whole project: the state of health, and everything associated with it, changes over time. It is reflected in every milestone of the roadmap.

title: Health is not stationary
text:
What nonstationarity means here
A quantity is stationary if its statistical properties — average level, variability, relationships with other variables — stay the same over time; nonstationary means they drift: the average moves, the variability changes, or the relationships themselves change (Box et al. 2015; Hyndman and Athanasopoulos 2021).
The project assumes BC’s health is nonstationary in all three senses:

The outcome drifts. Life expectancy, disease burden, mental health, and functional status trend, oscillate, and jump. Secular improvements, epidemics (including the COVID-19 pandemic (World Health Organization 2023) and the toxic drug crisis in BC (BC Centre for Disease Control, n.d.)), demographic aging, and policy or health-system reforms all move the level — sometimes gradually, sometimes as abrupt regime shifts.
Relationships drift. A variable associated with health in one decade need not be associated in the next. Income gradients, the effect of health-system capacity, and behavioural risk factors all operate in a changing context; a pooled estimate over many years may describe no actual period well.
The data-generating process drifts. Even when health itself is unchanged, the measurement changes: coding definitions, survey methods, coverage, and reporting practice evolve. Part of any apparent change in a series is change in how it was recorded.

title: Health is not stationary
text:
What this rules out
The intuitive way to report “the state of health” is a snapshot: this is BC’s number, here is how it compares. A dynamic view rejects the snapshot as the headline:

Levels without trajectories hide the direction. A stable-looking level can be the crossing point of rising and falling trends in subpopulations.
Single pooled estimates hide instability. A decade-long average association can be the blend of two periods with different — even opposite — relationships.
Undated conclusions rot. A finding true for 2000–2019 may be false for 2020 onward, but reads identically unless its window is stated.

title: Health is not stationary
section: What follows for each stage of the project
text:
What follows for each stage of the project

Definition (M1). Health is defined as a time-varying state with temporal semantics — a trajectory with levels, slopes, and possible discontinuities — not a timeless attribute.
Data (M2). Catalogues record coverage windows, refresh cadence, revisions, and definitional breaks; series are checked for structural breaks before use.
Description (M3). Trends, turning points, and change points are reported alongside levels; regimes (pre- and post-shock) are compared explicitly rather than blended.
Dependence (M4). Associations are estimated over stated windows and tested for stability before any pooled number is reported.
Causation (M5). Causal structures are time-indexed: lagged effects, feedback loops, and time-varying confounding are represented, and each causal claim carries a validity window.
Recommendations (M6). Every recommendation is dated, tied to the window of evidence behind it, and paired with the drift indicators that would trigger re-evaluation.

title: Health is not stationary
section: The practical consequence: re-run, don’t just publish once
text:
The practical consequence: re-run, don’t just publish once
If health is nonstationary, publishing an analysis is not the end of the job. The pipeline must be re-runnable as new data arrive, and results versioned with their observation window — so that “what is the state of health in BC?” can be answered again, differently, when it has changed. This is a cross-cutting concern in the roadmap: vigilance about drift applies to every milestone, not once at the end.

title: Defining health
text: Status: outline. The project’s provisional definition now lives at Definition of the state of health (milestone M1 in the roadmap); this page records the problem that definition has to solve.

title: Defining health
text:
Why define health first?
“State of health” sounds like something you could just measure. It is not. Before any indicator can be collected, compared over time, or used in a causal model, the project must commit to what counts as health and what does not — otherwise every downstream number rests on a different unstated assumption.
A definition is doing real work here. It determines:

What gets measured. Longevity only? Mental health? Functional capacity? Subjective wellbeing? Each choice admits some indicators and excludes others.
What comparisons mean. Two regions’ “health” are only comparable if both were measured against the same definition.
What the causal analysis is of. A causal model of health outcomes is undefined until the outcome is defined.

title: Defining health
section: What the definition must pin down
text:
What the definition must pin down
The definition document (M1) will commit to:

Conceptual basis — which established frameworks the definition builds on — e.g. the WHO definition of health as “a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being” (World Health Organization 1948), the ICF functioning model (World Health Organization 2001), capability approaches (Sen 1999) — and why.
Domains — the set of dimensions counted as part of the state of health (candidate families: mortality, morbidity, mental health, functional status, and context kept strictly separate from health itself).
Boundaries — what is explicitly excluded, and why (e.g. determinants of health are not health; health-system inputs are not health).
Unit of analysis — population-level vs. individual-level, and the geographic granularity the project works at.
Temporal semantics — health as a time-varying state: a trajectory with levels, slopes, and possible discontinuities, not a timeless attribute. Each domain declares its expected temporal behaviour (trending, seasonally varying, shock-prone, or plausibly stable), and the definition states how the project will detect when its description of health has gone stale (see Health is not stationary).
Operationalisation — for each domain, the candidate indicator families that can represent it with obtainable data — noting that data explaining BC’s health need not originate in BC (see Why BC only?).

title: Defining health
section: The hard boundary: health vs. its determinants
text:
The hard boundary: health vs. its determinants
The most common failure mode in “state of health” projects is quietly mixing health outcomes with their determinants (income, environment, service access). This project keeps them in separate layers: determinants enter the analysis as explanatory variables, never as components of health itself. The causal structures in milestone M5 depend on that distinction being drawn early.

Multi-objective and stochastic nature of recommendations
Improving the cumulative state of health is a multi-objective stochastic optimization problem. Different health domains compete for limited resources, and effects are uncertain. We must account for:

Multiple objectives: mortality, morbidity, functional status, mental health, subjective wellbeing, social wellbeing.
Uncertainty: parameter uncertainty, model uncertainty, and stochasticity in outcomes.
Time and dynamics: intertemporal trade-offs, discounting/weighting over cohorts and life course.
Constraints: resources, feasibility, equity (e.g. reducing disparities), and external validity.

Therefore, recommendations should be framed as candidate policies with Pareto frontiers and uncertainty intervals, not single “optimal” points.

    Plot.rectX([{x1: 2020, x2: 2024}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", fill: "grey", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
    Plot.ruleX(bySexTrend.levels.Males.change_points, {stroke: "red", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.ruleX(bySexTrend.levels.Females.change_points, {stroke: "steelblue", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),
    Plot.lineY(bySex, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", stroke: "sex", tip: true}),
    Plot.dot(bySex, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", stroke: "sex", tip: true})
  ]
})






The grey band marks the COVID-19 period (2020–2024); the red dashed lines are the male series’ regime breaks, the blue dotted lines the female series’. Life expectancy is a period measure: it is the average length of life a synthetic cohort would experience if it lived its whole life under the age-specific death rates of that year (Statistics Canada, n.d.).

title: Indicator: Life expectancy at birth, British Columbia
text:
Trajectory and regimes
Trend summaries, recomputed on every build (data/published/life_expectancy_bc_trend.json, data/published/life_expectancy_bc_by_sex_trend.json):

md`Over ${trend.start}–${trend.end} life expectancy at birth (both sexes)
changed by **${trend.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}** years per
decade, and the series is **${trend.stationarity.verdict}**. It carries a
monotone trend (Kendall's tau = ${trend.trend_test.tau.toFixed(2)},
p = ${trend.trend_test.p_value.toFixed(3)}) and departure from a single
straight line (residual-permutation test,
p = ${trend.break_test.p_value.toFixed(3)}). The BIC-selected regimes
break at ${trend.change_points.join(", ")}.`







sexRows = ["Males", "Females"].map(sex => ({
  sex,
  ...bySexTrend.levels[sex]
})).map(d => ({
  sex: d.sex,
  start: d.start,
  end: d.end,
  slope_per_decade: d.overall.slope_per_decade,
  verdict: d.stationarity.verdict,
  change_points: d.change_points.join(", ") || "—",
  change_point: d.change_point ?? "—"
}))
Inputs.table(sexRows, {
  columns: ["sex", "start", "end", "slope_per_decade", "verdict", "change_points", "change_point"],
  header: {sex: "sex", start: "from", end: "to", slope_per_decade: "slope/decade", verdict: "stationarity", change_points: "regime breaks", change_point: "largest break"}
})
















md`Both sex-specific series are **${bySexTrend.levels.Males.stationarity.verdict}** over
${bySexTrend.levels.Males.start}–${bySexTrend.levels.Males.end}. Females
live longer than males at every observed year, and the female advantage is
roughly constant in levels though not in the dating of its regimes. The
period includes the COVID-19 mortality shock, visible as the 2020–2022
dip; the pipeline dates it and does not attribute it.`






Method. Regimes are dated by a piecewise-linear segmentation, solved exactly by dynamic programming, with the number of breaks chosen by BIC; whether the series departs from one straight line is tested by residual permutation (Truong et al. 2020), and the trend by Kendall’s tau. Each series is therefore labelled stationary or not over its observed window, as milestone M3 requires. The full test output, including every candidate segmentation, is in the trend JSON. The permutation test assumes exchangeable residuals — autocorrelation is not modelled — so it is a test of departure from a linear trend, not a full time-series model.

title: Indicator: Life expectancy at birth, British Columbia
text:
Caveats

Period, not cohort. Life expectancy at birth is a period life-table quantity: it is not the expected lifespan of anyone actually born in that year, and it says nothing about the health of the living (Statistics Canada, n.d.).
Break detection, not explanation. The regimes are dated by a formal test (above); the test says a break beyond a single straight line exists, not what caused it. Recent-year estimates rest on few data points and are the least certain.
Sex categories are the source’s. The table publishes both sexes, males, and females; the pipeline reports these as given.
Coverage. The source series is 1980–2024 and excludes Prince Edward Island from the published table; the BC series itself is complete. This table has no sub-provincial rows — health-authority and regional life tables are separate Statistics Canada products.
Revisions. Statistics Canada may revise recent-year estimates; the published files are regenerated from the source on each build.

title: Glossary
text:
Terms are listed alphabetically. This glossary grows with milestone M1 (definition) in the roadmap.

Causal structure

A representation (typically a directed acyclic graph, or DAG) of the assumed cause-and-effect relationships among variables, used to reason about what interventions would change health outcomes (Pearl 2009).

Construct

The thing a measurement is intended to represent — for example the state of health, or one of its domains. Constructs are real but not directly observable; measurements of them are proxies. See the definition of the state of health.

Data

Construed broadly: any publicly available information that can be appropriately used for the project’s goals — from microdata through published summary statistics, indicator tables, dashboards, and report figures.

Definition (provisional)

The project’s working definition of the state of health. It is versioned and expected to evolve as the project learns what is measurable; each revision records its trigger and its changes. See the definition document.

Diátaxis

The documentation framework this site follows, organising docs into four modes: tutorials, how-to guides, reference, and explanation (Procida, n.d.).

Health authority

One of the regional organisations delivering health services in BC (e.g. Vancouver Coastal Health, Fraser Health) (Government of British Columbia, Ministry of Health, n.d.). A common geographic breakdown for BC health data.

Indicator

A defined, sourced, reproducible measurement used to represent some aspect of the state of health (e.g. life expectancy at birth). An indicator is a proxy, never the construct itself.

Measurement framework

The scheme of domains and candidate indicators that operationalises the project’s definition of the state of health. See the measurement framework.

Multilevel model

A statistical model in which data at more than one level of resolution (e.g. individuals within regions) are modelled jointly, allowing information to be shared across levels (Gelman and Hill 2007). One of the ways the project fuses pictures at different resolutions.

Nonstationarity

The property of a series or relationship whose statistical properties (level, variability, association with other variables) change over time (Box et al. 2015; Hyndman and Athanasopoulos 2021). The project assumes BC’s health is nonstationary in all three senses; see Health is not stationary.

Observation window

The time period a reported result was estimated on. Every published figure in this project carries its observation window, because a result true for one window may not hold for another.

Proxy

A measurement used in place of a construct that cannot be observed directly — every indicator in this project is a proxy. Proxies carry measurement error and construct error, and can drift over time; they are never identical with the state of health they track. See Proxies are not the state of health.

Regime shift

An abrupt change in the level or behaviour of a series — e.g. an epidemic, health system reform, or coding definition change — after which the series is effectively a different one. Comparisons spanning a regime shift are treated separately from comparisons within a regime.

Resolution

The level at which a datum or result is observed — individual, neighbourhood, HSDA, health authority, provincial, or external/non-BC. This project uses all available resolutions and records the resolution of every result.

State of health (SoH)

The condition of health in a population at a point in time and space — the central quantity this project describes and predicts. Defined provisionally in the definition document.

Stationarity

The opposite of nonstationarity: a series or relationship whose statistical properties hold steady over the analysis window. Pooled single estimates are only reported when stationarity is supported (Box et al. 2015; Hyndman and Athanasopoulos 2021); see Health is not stationary.






References

Box, George E. P., Gwilym M. Jenkins, Gregory C. Reinsel, and Greta M. Ljung. 2015. Time Series Analysis: Forecasting and Control. 5th ed. John Wiley & Sons.


Gelman, Andrew, and Jennifer Hill. 2007. Data Analysis Using Regression and Multilevel/Hierarchical Models. Cambridge University Press.


Government of British Columbia, Ministry of Health. n.d. Health Authorities. Accessed October 18, 2026. https://www2.gov.bc.ca/gov/content/health/about-bc-s-health-care-system/partners/health-authorities.


Hyndman, Rob J., and George Athanasopoulos. 2021. Forecasting: Principles and Practice. 3rd ed. OTexts. https://otexts.com/fpp3/.


Pearl, Judea. 2009. Causality: Models, Reasoning, and Inference. 2nd ed. Cambridge University Press.


Procida, Daniele. n.d. Diátaxis: A Systematic Approach to Technical Documentation. Accessed October 18, 2026. https://diataxis.fr.

Provenance

title: Indicator: Mortality rates, British Columbia
text:
Trend

rows = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc.csv").csv({typed: true})
rates = rows.filter(d => d.characteristic === "Mortality rate per 1,000 population" && d.age_group === "Age at time of death, all ages" && d.sex === "Both sexes")
bySexRates = rows.filter(d => d.characteristic === "Mortality rate per 1,000 population" && d.age_group === "Age at time of death, all ages" && d.sex !== "Both sexes")
counts = rows.filter(d => d.characteristic === "Number of deaths" && d.sex === "Both sexes")
asr = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised.csv").csv({typed: true}).filter(d => d.sex === "Both sexes")
bySexAsr = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised.csv").csv({typed: true}).filter(d => d.sex !== "Both sexes")
trend = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_trend.json").json()
asrTrend = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised_trend.json").json()
bySexTrend = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_rates_bc_by_sex_trend.json").json()
series = rates.map(d => ({year: d.ref_date, rate: d.value, series: "Crude"}))
  .concat(asr.map(d => ({year: d.ref_date, rate: d.value, series: "Age-standardised"})))








































































Plot.plot({
  title: "Mortality rate, British Columbia (per 1,000 population)",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "Deaths per 1,000 population"},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.rectX([{x1: 2020, x2: 2025}], {x1: "x1", x2: "x2", fill: "grey", fillOpacity: 0.12}),
    Plot.ruleX(trend.change_points, {stroke: "red", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.ruleX(asrTrend.change_points, {stroke: "steelblue", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),
    Plot.lineY(series, {x: "year", y: "rate", stroke: "series", tip: true}),
    Plot.dot(series, {x: "year", y: "rate", stroke: "series", tip: true})
  ]
})






The crude rate is per 1,000 residents at the observed age mix; the age-standardised rate applies the WHO World Standard Population (2000–2025) (Ahmad et al. 2001), removing the effect of BC’s ageing population. The grey band marks the COVID-19 period (2020–2024); the red dashed lines are the crude rate’s regime breaks, the blue dotted lines the age-standardised rate’s.

Plot.plot({
  title: "Number of deaths, British Columbia",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "Deaths"},
  marks: [
    Plot.lineY(counts, {x: "ref_date", y: "value"}),
    Plot.dot(counts, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", tip: true})

})

title: Indicator: Mortality rates, British Columbia
text:
Trajectory and regimes
Trend summaries, recomputed on every build (data/published/mortality_rates_bc_trend.json, data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised_trend.json):

segments = trend.segments.length
  ? trend.segments
  : [{label: "whole series", start: trend.start, end: trend.end, ...trend.overall}]
Inputs.table(segments, {
  columns: ["label", "start", "end", "slope_per_year", "slope_per_decade", "fitted_start", "fitted_end", "change_within"],
  header: {label: "crude segment", start: "from", end: "to", slope_per_year: "slope/yr", slope_per_decade: "slope/decade", fitted_start: "level at start", fitted_end: "level at end", change_within: "change within"}
})
















jumpRows = trend.jumps.length
  ? trend.jumps.map(j => ({year: j.year, previous_level: j.previous_level, next_level: j.next_level, jump: j.jump}))
  : [{year: "—", previous_level: "—", next_level: "—", jump: 0}]
Inputs.table(jumpRows, {
  columns: ["year", "previous_level", "next_level", "jump"],
  header: {year: "break", previous_level: "level before", next_level: "level after", jump: "level jump"}
})
















dc = trend.decomposition
md`The break at **${trend.change_point}** is mostly a change of
**slope**, not of level: the total change of
${dc.observed_change.toFixed(2)} decomposes into
${dc.within_regime_change.toFixed(2)} within the regimes and
${dc.between_regime_change.toFixed(2)} in level jumps at the breaks.`
















md`Over ${trend.start}–${trend.end} the crude rate changed by
**${trend.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}** per 1,000 per decade, and the
series is **${trend.stationarity.verdict}**.
It carries a monotone trend (Kendall's tau = ${trend.trend_test.tau.toFixed(2)},
p = ${trend.trend_test.p_value.toFixed(3)}) and departure from a single straight
line (residual-permutation test, p = ${trend.break_test.p_value.toFixed(3)}).
The BIC-selected regimes break at ${trend.change_points.join(", ")}, the largest
slope change at **${trend.change_point}**${trend.change_point === 2020 ? " — the onset of the COVID-19 period" : ""}.`






The age-standardised rate tells a different story, because it is the one that abstracts from population ageing:

asrSegments = asrTrend.segments
Inputs.table(asrSegments, {
  columns: ["label", "start", "end", "slope_per_year", "slope_per_decade"],
  header: {label: "standardised segment", start: "from", end: "to", slope_per_year: "slope/yr", slope_per_decade: "slope/decade"}
})
















md`The age-standardised rate is **${asrTrend.stationarity.verdict}**
(Kendall's tau = ${asrTrend.trend_test.tau.toFixed(2)},
p = ${asrTrend.trend_test.p_value.toFixed(3)}; break test
p = ${asrTrend.break_test.p_value.toFixed(3)}), with a regime break at
**${asrTrend.change_point}**: the decline reverses there — the standardised
rate fell before it and has risen since.`






Method. Regimes are dated by a piecewise-linear segmentation, solved exactly by dynamic programming, with the number of breaks chosen by BIC; whether the series departs from one straight line is tested by residual permutation (Truong et al. 2020), and the trend by Kendall’s tau. Each series is therefore labelled stationary or not over its observed window, as milestone M3 requires. The full test output, including every candidate segmentation, is in the trend JSON. The permutation test assumes exchangeable residuals — autocorrelation is not modelled — so it is a test of departure from a linear trend, not a full time-series model.

title: Indicator: Mortality rates, British Columbia
text:
Sex breakdown
The source table publishes males and females separately; both are built through the same pipeline, including per-sex age standardisation, and each carries its own stationarity verdict (data/published/mortality_rates_bc_by_sex_trend.json).

Plot.plot({
  title: "Crude mortality rate by sex, British Columbia (per 1,000 population)",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "Deaths per 1,000 population"},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(bySexTrend.crude.Males.change_points, {stroke: "red", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.lineY(bySexRates, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", stroke: "sex", tip: true}),
    Plot.dot(bySexRates, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", stroke: "sex", tip: true})
  ]
})







Plot.plot({
  title: "Age-standardised mortality rate by sex, British Columbia (per 1,000 population)",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "Deaths per 1,000 population"},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [
    Plot.ruleX(bySexTrend.age_standardised.Males.change_points, {stroke: "red", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.ruleX(bySexTrend.age_standardised.Females.change_points, {stroke: "steelblue", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),
    Plot.lineY(bySexAsr, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", stroke: "sex", tip: true}),
    Plot.dot(bySexAsr, {x: "ref_date", y: "value", stroke: "sex", tip: true})
  ]
})







sexRows = ["Males", "Females"].flatMap(sex => [
  {series: "Crude", sex, ...bySexTrend.crude[sex]},
  {series: "Age-standardised", sex, ...bySexTrend.age_standardised[sex]}
]).map(d => ({
  series: d.series,
  sex: d.sex,
  slope_per_decade: d.overall.slope_per_decade,
  verdict: d.stationarity.verdict,
  change_points: d.change_points.join(", ") || "—",
  change_point: d.change_point ?? "—"
}))
Inputs.table(sexRows, {
  columns: ["series", "sex", "slope_per_decade", "verdict", "change_points", "change_point"],
  header: {series: "series", sex: "sex", slope_per_decade: "slope/decade", verdict: "stationarity", change_points: "regime breaks", change_point: "largest break"}
})
















md`Every sex-specific series is nonstationary over ${bySexTrend.crude.Males.start}–${bySexTrend.crude.Males.end}.
Males sit above females on both crude and standardised rates throughout, and
the standardised decline-then-reversal appears in both sexes, but the
standardised turnaround is dated **${bySexTrend.age_standardised.Males.change_point}**
for males and **${bySexTrend.age_standardised.Females.change_point}** for females —
close to, but not identical with, the both-sexes date of
${asrTrend.change_point}; the sexes should be read as separate trajectories,
not one trend disaggregated after the fact.`

title: Indicator: Mortality rates, British Columbia
text:
Age breakdown
The same source carries every five-year age group. Each is built into its own trajectory, so we can ask whether the decline is general or driven by particular ages (data/published/mortality_age_specific_bc_by_age_trend.json; generated by uv run sohbc build mortality_age_specific_bc).

byAge = FileAttachment("../data/published/mortality_age_specific_bc_by_age_trend.json").json()
ageRows = rows.filter(d => d.characteristic === "Mortality rate per 1,000 population" && d.sex === "Both sexes" && d.age_group !== "Age at time of death, all ages" && d.age_group !== "Age at time of death, not stated")
ageOrder = ["under 1 year", "1 to 4 years", "5 to 9 years", "10 to 14 years", "15 to 19 years", "20 to 24 years", "25 to 29 years", "30 to 34 years", "35 to 39 years", "40 to 44 years", "45 to 49 years", "50 to 54 years", "55 to 59 years", "60 to 64 years", "65 to 69 years", "70 to 74 years", "75 to 79 years", "80 to 84 years", "85 to 89 years", "90 years and over"]
short = g => g.replace("Age at time of death, ", "")






























Plot.plot({
  title: "Mortality rate by age group, both sexes (per 1,000; 5-year bands)",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {label: null, domain: ageOrder.slice().reverse()},
  color: {scheme: "YlGnBu", legend: true, label: "per 1,000"},
  marks: [
    Plot.cell(ageRows, {x: "ref_date", y: d => short(d.age_group), fill: "value", tip: true})
  ],
  width: 900
})







ageSummary = ageOrder.map(g => {
  const t = byAge["Both sexes"][`Age at time of death, ${g}`]
  return t && {
    age: g,
    slope_per_decade: t.overall.slope_per_decade,
    verdict: t.stationarity.verdict,
    change_point: t.change_point ?? "—"
  }
}).filter(Boolean)
Inputs.table(ageSummary, {
  columns: ["age", "slope_per_decade", "verdict", "change_point"],
  header: {age: "age group", slope_per_decade: "slope/decade (per 1,000)", verdict: "stationarity", change_point: "largest break"}
})
















oldest = byAge["Both sexes"]["Age at time of death, 90 years and over"]
youngest = byAge["Both sexes"]["Age at time of death, 30 to 34 years"]
md`The decline is real at **every** age, but its size scales with age:
about **${oldest.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(1)}** per 1,000 per decade
at 90 and over, against roughly **${youngest.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}**
at 30–34. The all-ages crude rate discussed above mixes these: an ageing
population shifts weight toward the high-rate old groups, so the all-ages
crude rate can rise even while every age-specific rate falls. This is the
same ageing signature seen in the crude-versus-standardised contrast,
decomposed by age.`






















Method. Each age group is summarised by the same :func:~sohbc.indicators.trajectory routine as the headline series (piecewise-linear regimes by BIC, residual-permutation break test, Kendall-tau trend). Because there are 20 groups, the age-specific build uses 199 permutations rather than the headline 1,999; this coarsens the p-value but not the regime dating. Small counts in the youngest groups make their rates volatile, so their slopes and breaks are weakly identified.

title: Indicator: Mortality rates, British Columbia
text:
Caveats

Crude vs standardised. Two series are published: the crude rate (observed age mix) and a directly age-standardised rate using the WHO World Standard Population (2000–2025) (Ahmad et al. 2001). The crude rate can rise while the standardised rate falls if the population ages — seen here, so read the two together.
Break detection, not explanation. The regimes are dated by a formal test (above) (Truong et al. 2020); the test says that a break beyond a single straight line exists, not what caused it, and the 2020–2024 regime rests on five annual points, so its slope is the least certain.
The standardised turnaround predates the pandemic. The age-standardised rate’s regime break falls at 2013, before the COVID-19 period, so the pandemic does not explain the reversal on its own; the pipeline dates the change and does not attribute it.
Observation window and regimes. The series spans 1991–2024 and crosses the COVID-19 period (2020–2024), marked on the figure.
Sex categories are the source’s. The table publishes both sexes, males, and females; the pipeline reports these categories as given and does not model sex or gender beyond them.
Resolution. Published at provincial resolution, with age-group rows (both sexes) and male/female breakdowns in the tidy file, and age-specific trajectories in a separate summary. Sub-provincial views are a separate indicator.
Revisions. Statistics Canada may revise recent-year estimates; the published files are regenerated from the source on each build.

title: Indicator: Mortality rates, British Columbia
text:
Reproduce
uv run sohbc fetch statcan_wds
uv run sohbc build mortality_rates_bc mortality_age_specific_bc
The tidy dataset is published at data/published/mortality_rates_bc.csv (all ages and age groups, by sex), with the age-standardised series — one row per year and sex — at data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised.csv (standard population weights in data/reference/who_standard_population.csv). The headline trend tests are at data/published/mortality_rates_bc_trend.json and data/published/mortality_rates_bc_age_standardised_trend.json, and the per-sex tests at data/published/mortality_rates_bc_by_sex_trend.json.

title: Reference
text:
Available reference

Glossary
Definitions of the terms this project uses consistently.


Measurement framework
Domains mapped to candidate indicator families and likely sources (provisional, milestone M1).


Data sources

Data quality
Known gaps, revisions, suppressions, and definitional breaks in the catalogued sources.


State of health in BC: a descriptive report
The first edition of the project’s descriptive report (milestone M3): trends, sex breakdowns, and stated observation windows across the published indicators.


Indicator: Mortality rates, British Columbia
The project’s first published indicator, with provenance, caveats, and a regenerable chart.


Indicator: Life expectancy at birth, British Columbia

The project’s first sub-provincial indicator: age-standardised premature and potentially avoidable mortality across BC’s health authorities and health service delivery areas (2021/2023).


Indicator: Life satisfaction, British Columbia
Life satisfaction among BC adults (2015–2024) from the Canadian Community Health Survey, the first published indicator outside the mortality domain.


Indicator family: Health survey indicators, British Columbia
Ten BC survey series (physical morbidity, mental health, subjective and social wellbeing, access to care) drawn from one Statistics Canada table, with their trend and regime summaries side by side.


Project structure
What lives where in the repository and how the documentation site is organised.


Planned

Data source catalogue — every data source: coverage, licence, access route, refresh cadence, and source form (microdata, summary statistics, dashboard, or report). “Data” is construed broadly: the aim is the best use of all publicly available information that can be appropriately used (milestone M2).
Indicator reference pages — one page per indicator: definition, unit, population, provenance, caveats (milestones M1–M3).
Methods reference — statistical and causal methods used, with parameters (milestones M4–M5).

title: Data quality
text: Status: v0.1 (milestone M2 in progress). This is the project’s running register of known problems with the data sources. It is expected to grow as sources are ingested in earnest.

title: Data quality
text:
What this report covers
The roadmap asks for a register of known gaps, revisions, suppressions, and definitional breaks. Anything that would mislead a reader who trusted a number at face value belongs here.

title: Data quality
text:
Known gaps

Determinants and stratifiers. Income, education, and employment are used to stratify results (see the measurement framework); BC Stats, the BC Data Catalogue, Statistics Canada, and K-12 reporting are catalogued as their sources. They are determinants, not health outcomes, and are never reported as health on their own.
Microdata access. Individual-level sources are catalogued as access routes (Population Data BC; Statistics Canada Research Data Centres) but no approvals are in place yet, so the catalogue is aggregate-only in practice. Nothing individual-level may enter the repository regardless.
Neighbourhood-level health indicators. Population denominators exist at LHA/neighbourhood resolution, but health outcomes are not yet catalogued below health-authority level.
External drivers. Cross-border patient flows and supply-chain pressures are identified as relevant but have no catalogued source yet; the wildfire, demographic, and macro series are the current stand-ins.
Social wellbeing. Measures of social connection and belonging are sparse and carried on a small number of survey series only.

title: Data quality
text:
Revisions and provisional figures

Substance-use mortality is published provisionally and revised upward as investigations conclude (BC Centre for Disease Control, n.d.). Preliminary and final figures must never be pooled without noting the vintage.
Cancer statistics for the most recent years are typically incomplete because of registration lag (BC Cancer, Provincial Health Services Authority, n.d.).
Population estimates at sub-provincial levels are revised as administrative sources update; rates computed on them inherit the revision.
National survey estimates carry sampling error and are occasionally revised after release (Statistics Canada, n.d.).

title: Data quality
text:
Suppression

Small-area counts (e.g. vital statistics by small geography) are suppressed for privacy (BC Stats, Government of British Columbia, n.d.). Suppressed cells are missing, not zero; treating them as zero biases rates.

title: Data quality
text:
Definitional breaks (regime shifts)
These are candidates for the regime-aware reporting required by milestone M3; each marks a point where a series before and after is effectively different. The pipeline dates regime breaks from the data itself (piecewise-linear segmentation with BIC selection, plus a permutation test for a break beyond a linear trend); the table below records the known causes behind such breaks, which the statistical test can locate but cannot name.








Break
Affected sources
Implication




Cause-of-death coding revisions (ICD revisions)
Vital Statistics; national mortality
Cause-specific mortality series are not directly comparable across the revision boundary


Declared public-health emergency (2016)
BCCDC substance-use dashboard; overdose response
Surveillance expanded at the emergency; counts before and after reflect different detection intensity


COVID-19 pandemic (2020–)
mortality, morbidity, mental health
Both a real shock and a measurement shock (care disruption, coding changes)


Survey redesigns (e.g. Canadian Community Health Survey)
Statistics Canada health series
Break in trend; pre- and post-redesign estimates differ


Indicator-definition updates
CIHI indicators
Rebased or redefined indicators reset their own series

title: Data quality
text:
URL verification
As part of M2, every catalogued URL was checked for reachability with uv run sohbc check --all. All catalogued landing pages and the automated download endpoints returned HTTP 200 at the time of checking (28 sources). The federal publisher’s own portal was unreachable from the verification environment, so federal open data is reached through the Open Government portal record instead; this is noted on that catalogue entry.

title: Data quality
text:
First published indicator
The first end-to-end indicator — provincial mortality rates from Statistics Canada table 13-10-0710-01 — is built by the pipeline, including male/female breakdowns and per-sex age standardisation. Its known limitations (provincial resolution only, source sex categories, spans the COVID-19 period, subject to revision) are recorded on the indicator page and are examples of the kind of entry this register is meant to capture. Its regime breaks are dated by the formal tests documented on that page rather than read off by eye.
A second indicator, life expectancy at birth by sex (Statistics Canada table 13-10-0837-01), is now built through the same pipeline; it shares the mortality domain and the same caveat classes (period measure, revision of recent years, COVID-19 period, source sex categories). The source table has no sub-provincial rows.
A third source, Statistics Canada table 13-10-0905-01, supplies a family of survey indicators that widen the framework beyond mortality: life satisfaction and mental health series among them. Survey estimates bring caveat classes the administrative tables did not: sampling error, coefficient-of-variation suppression (flagged cells), and a collection-frame change mid-series, so a step in the series may be a step in the measurement. These are recorded on the indicator pages.
A fourth source takes the project below the province: Statistics Canada table 13-10-0931-01 supplies age-standardised premature and potentially avoidable mortality for BC’s five health authorities and 17 health service delivery areas. It adds two caveat classes of its own — health-region boundaries that change across table vintages, and rates published only as overlapping three-year averages, so the source supports a regional snapshot but not a regional trajectory; the trend machinery is therefore not applied to it.

title: Data quality
text:
Governance

Licences vary by source (open-government licences to publisher terms). Each catalogue entry records its licence; redistribution of anything committed must respect it.
No individual-level data in the repository — a hard rule.
First Nations data are governed by the First Nations principles of OCAP® and specific agreements; they are cited for context, not redistributed (First Nations Information Governance Centre, n.d.).
“Best use” standard. A source backed only by published summary statistics is admissible when it passes licence and governance checks — the goal is the best use of all publicly available information that can be appropriately used.

title: Data quality
text:
Keeping this current
Add an entry here whenever ingesting a source surfaces a problem, and update the catalogue when a gap closes. See How to ingest a source.

title: How to ingest a data source
text:

uv run sohbc fetch <key>
The file lands in data/raw/<key>/ and an entry is written to data/manifest.json with its URL, size, and SHA-256 checksum. data/raw/ and the manifest are not committed — the data is reproducible from the catalogue, not stored in git.
For a source you must retrieve by hand (most dashboards and portals), leave download.kind: manual and place the downloaded file under data/raw/<key>/ yourself, or record the access route in form_of_access.

title: How to ingest a data source
text:
5. Record problems
If the source has suppressions, provisional figures, or breaks, add them to the data quality report.

title: How to ingest a data source
text:
6. Check governance
Confirm the licence permits what you intend to do, and that no individual-level data is committed. First Nations data require governance review before use (First Nations Information Governance Centre, n.d.).

text:
7. Render and verify
quarto render
Then wire the source into the indicator page (How to add an indicator) and the descriptive pipeline (milestone M3).

title: State-of-Health BC
text:
State-of-Health BC (SoHBC) is a project that attempts to describe and predict the state of health in British Columbia, Canada — from defining what “health” means here, through the data and causal structures behind it, to actions that would improve it.
The project is early stage. This site is the project’s documentation and will grow alongside the analysis.
Two principles frame everything here. Health is treated as dynamic and nonstationary — a trajectory that changes over time, along with the relationships behind it (why). And while the object of study is BC’s health, the data explaining it are not limited to BC-origin data (why).

title: State-of-Health BC

The journey

Defining health, and the state of health in BC.
Finding and exploring data that describe the state of health in BC over time and space — “data” construed broadly, from microdata to published summary statistics.
Characterising the variables that are statistically dependent with health.

title: Tutorial: Your first look at BC health data
text:
Status: available for the two published indicators (mortality rates and life expectancy). The regional-comparison step awaits sub-provincial ingestion (milestone M3 in the roadmap).
In this tutorial you will fetch a headline health indicator for British Columbia, build it from source into a tidy dataset, and look at its trajectory — using only reproducible, documented steps. No prior familiarity with the project is assumed.

title: Tutorial: Your first look at BC health data
text:
Prerequisites

A working environment (see How to contribute): Quarto and uv installed, uv sync run once.
No data needs to be present beforehand — we fetch it in step 2.

title: Tutorial: Your first look at BC health data
section: 1. See what the project knows about
text:
1. See what the project knows about
Lists the indicators the pipeline can build, and the catalogued data sources behind them:
uv run sohbc indicators
uv run sohbc list
indicators lists the entries the pipeline can build — mortality rates, life expectancy, a sub-provincial mortality-inequality view, and a family of survey indicators (life satisfaction, perceived health and mental health, anxiety and mood disorders, diabetes, high blood pressure, having a regular provider, daily smoking) — each tagged with its measurement-framework domain. list shows the catalogued sources; only a few are marked auto (the pipeline can fetch them without a browser).

title: Tutorial: Your first look at BC health data
text:
2. Fetch the raw source
Each indicator names a catalogued source. Life expectancy comes from Statistics Canada’s life tables. Fetch it into the reproducible local layout:
uv run sohbc fetch statcan_life_tables
The raw response lands in data/raw/statcan_life_tables/ and a checksum is recorded in data/manifest.json. Raw data is not committed: the catalogue and this command are what make it reproducible.

title: Tutorial: Your first look at BC health data
text:
3. Build the tidy dataset
Turn the raw table into a published, tidy dataset:
uv run sohbc build life_expectancy_bc
This writes data/published/life_expectancy_bc.csv plus trend-test JSON. Look at the first rows:
head -4 data/published/life_expectancy_bc.csv
Every datum carries its reference date, geography, age group, sex, and characteristic, so nothing about its resolution is lost (a project rule — see the measurement framework).

title: Tutorial: Your first look at BC health data
text:
4. Look at the trajectory
Load the tidy file and plot the series in the language of your choice. The R-and-Python-agnostic view is simply to read the published chart on the indicator’s reference page, which is regenerated from the same files on every render.
To make your own view, the two headline characteristics are:

Life expectancy (in years) at age x (ex) with age_group == "0 years" — life expectancy at birth.
Number of deaths and Mortality rate per 1,000 population in data/published/mortality_rates_bc.csv — the mortality indicator.

Two habits the project expects of any view you build:

Plot the whole window, not one point. The trajectory JSON alongside each CSV states whether the series is stationary over its window and, if not, where the regimes break. Read the number and its window.
Mark the regimes. The COVID-19 period (2020–2024) is shaded on the published charts; regime breaks are drawn as dashed lines. A series that moves is not necessarily a series whose rule changed — the tests distinguish the two.

title: Tutorial: Your first look at BC health data
text:
5. Read the caveats
Open the indicator’s reference page and read its provenance table and caveats. For life expectancy, the key caveat is that it is a period measure — the average lifespan of a synthetic cohort under one year’s death rates (Statistics Canada, n.d.) — not anyone’s expected lifespan and not a statement about the health of the living.

title: Tutorial: Your first look at BC health data
text:
6. Reflect
Note what the chart does not tell you. Life expectancy at birth says nothing about morbidity, functional status, or wellbeing; a rising value can coexist with worsening health among the living. This is exactly why the project treats every indicator as a proxy for a domain, never the state of health itself — the explanation section takes this up.

title: Tutorial: Your first look at BC health data
text:
What you have learned
The whole project follows the pattern you just walked: a catalogued source → a fetch step → a reproducible build into tidy data with its resolution recorded → a trajectory view that states its window and regimes → a proxy that is read alongside its caveats. Every later indicator and analysis reuses it.

title: Tutorial: Your first look at BC health data
text:
Next steps

Add an indicator of your own.
Ingest a data source into the catalogue.
Regional comparison — the roadmap’s M3 outstanding work — is where this tutorial’s target structure originally pointed; it needs sub-provincial ingestion first.

Each slope is in percentage points per decade over 2015–2024, for both
sexes; a positive slope is not automatically good or bad — the *better
if…* column states the direction that the measurement treats as
favourable. `stationarity` is the pipeline's label from the formal tests
(stationary, nonstationary, or undetermined where the series is too short
for the test to have power); `largest break` is the BIC-selected change
point, where one exists.

## What the family shows

The series are not all moving the same way, and the direction of movement
follows the direction of the measurement:

- **Wellbeing is falling.** Life satisfaction (`-11.5` pp/decade;
  break at 2020) and sense of belonging (`-10.6` pp/decade; break at
  2020) both fell sharply, and both are dated to 2020 by the pipeline.
- **Poor self-rated state is rising.** Perceived mental health fair or
  poor rose `+13.9` pp/decade and perceived health fair or poor `+4.7`
  pp/decade; both are nonstationary.
- **Mental-health conditions are rising.** Anxiety (`+8.4` pp/decade) and
  mood disorders (`+5.5` pp/decade, break at 2020) both increased.
- **Some behaviours improve.** Daily smoking fell `-4.4` pp/decade, though
  the regime split at 2020 shows the decline flattening after 2020
  (`-7.3` before, `-1.0` after).
- **Two series are flat.** Diabetes (`+0.8`) and having a regular
  healthcare provider (`-2.1`) are labelled **stationary** over the
  window — no evidence of a trend beyond year-to-year noise.

Read together, the family is a picture of rising self-reported distress
and falling life evaluation over a decade, with the clearest breaks
coinciding with 2020. The pipeline dates those breaks; this page does not
claim they are caused by the pandemic.

## Caveats

- **Survey estimate.** Every series is self-reported on a national survey,
  carrying sampling error and a coefficient-of-variation release policy;
  some cells are suppressed or flagged. Plotted values are published point
  estimates.
- **Measurement, not only change.** The CCHS collection frame changed over
  2015–2024 and 2020–2021 collection was disrupted by the pandemic. A
  step in a series may be a step in the measurement. Direction of the
  breaks is dated, not attributed.
- **Short window.** Ten annual points is a short series; the
  stationarity test has limited power, which is why some series are
  labelled *undetermined* rather than stationary.
- **Self-report and definition drift.** "Percent" mixes reported
  behaviour, diagnosed conditions, and self-rated state; each has a
  different relationship to health, and a survey question that changes
  wording does not change meaninglessly.
- **No sub-provincial rows.** Provincial only; regional survey series are
  separate products.
- **Revisions.** Statistics Canada may revise estimates; the published
  files are regenerated from the source on each build.

## Reproduce

```bash
uv run sohbc fetch statcan_health_indicators
uv run sohbc build
Every series publishes data/published/<key>.csv, data/published/<key>_trend.json, and data/published/<key>_by_sex_trend.json. The selection and definitions are in src/sohbc/indicators.py; add or remove a series there and rebuild.

from ${trend.segments[1].start}.`

  sex,
  ...bySexTrend.levels[sex]
})).map(d => ({
  sex: d.sex,
  slope_per_decade: d.overall.slope_per_decade,
  verdict: d.stationarity.verdict,

Method. Regimes are dated by a piecewise-linear segmentation, solved exactly by dynamic programming, with the number of breaks chosen by BIC; whether the series departs from one straight line is tested by residual permutation (Truong et al. 2020), and the trend by Kendall’s tau. Each series is therefore labelled stationary or not over its observed window, as milestone M3 requires. The full test output, including every candidate segmentation, is in the trend JSON. The permutation test assumes exchangeable residuals — autocorrelation is not modelled — so it is a test of departure from a linear trend, not a full time-series model.

title: Indicator: Life satisfaction, British Columbia
text:
Caveats

Survey estimate. Life satisfaction is self-reported on a national survey; it carries sampling error and a coefficient-of-variation release policy, so individual cells may be suppressed or flagged. The plotted series are the published point estimates.
Measurement, not only change. The CCHS collection frame changed over 2015–2024 and 2020–2021 collection was disrupted by the pandemic. Part of the 2020 break may be a change in how the series was measured, not only in how people answered. The pipeline dates the break; it does not attribute it.
Break detection, not explanation. The regimes are dated by a formal test (above); the test says a break beyond a single straight line exists, not what caused it.
Sex categories are the source’s. The table publishes both sexes, males, and females; the pipeline reports these as given.
No sub-provincial rows. The source table is provincial only; health-authority and regional survey series are separate products.
Revisions. Statistics Canada may revise survey estimates; the published files are regenerated from the source on each build.

title: breaks
text:
breaks
Formal change-point detection and trend testing for indicator series.
The descriptive trajectory summary in :mod:sohbc.indicators reports a single best split by eye; this module supplies the formal tests milestone M3 calls for, so every series can be labelled stationary or not and its regimes dated with stated uncertainty.



Segmentation. The series is modelled as piecewise linear (a trend break changes the slope): the optimal segmentation for a given number of breaks is found with the dynamic-programming solver of ruptures (Truong et al. 2020), using its linear cost — the residual sum of squares of a straight-line fit within each segment.
Number of breaks. Chosen by BIC over 0..max_breaks regimes, each extra break paying for two regression parameters plus the break location. This avoids an arbitrary penalty scale: the penalty is derived from the likelihood, not tuned.
Is there a break at all? A permutation test against a single linear trend. The statistic is the reduction in residual sum of squares from the best split; the null distribution resamples the residuals of the global linear fit (preserving the trend, destroying any break). This tests “no break beyond a straight line”, which is exactly the null the trajectory summary assumes away.
Trend/stationarity. Kendall’s tau on (year, value) gives a rank-based monotone-trend test; a series is labelled nonstationary when either test is significant, and the reasons are recorded.

All randomness is seeded, so published results reproduce exactly.

md`Across **${prem.n_regions}** service delivery areas in
${prem.ref_date}, premature mortality ranges from
**${prem.lowest.value.toFixed(1)}** in
${prem.lowest.region.replace(" Health Service Delivery Area", "")} to
**${prem.highest.value.toFixed(1)}** in
${prem.highest.region.replace(" Health Service Delivery Area", "")}, a
ratio of **${prem.ratio.toFixed(1)}** (mean
${prem.mean.toFixed(0)}). Potentially avoidable mortality is more unequal
still at **${avoid.ratio.toFixed(1)}×**. The northern and interior service
delivery areas sit highest and the Vancouver-metro areas lowest.`






Method. Dispersion is computed per cause, sex, and reference period at the service-delivery-area level, so authorities are not double-counted alongside the areas they contain. The published files hold every region and period; the JSON summary holds the sorted values, the extremes, the ratio, the range, and the mean. No regime test is run: the source is three-year averages over two overlapping periods.

title: Indicator: Mortality inequality across BC health regions
text:
Caveats

Cross-sectional, not a trajectory. The source publishes three-year averages only, so this indicator dates the regional gap but cannot show how it moved. The trend indicators carry the temporal story.
Boundaries move. Health-region boundaries changed across table vintages; the 2023 boundary set is used here. Comparisons across vintages are not like-for-like.
Overlapping intervals. Every rate carries a 95% confidence interval and neighbouring regions’ intervals overlap, so the ordering in the middle of the distribution is not sharp. The gap between the extremes is.
Small-area suppression. Some area/period/sex cells are suppressed for reliability, so the number of areas reported varies by stratum.
Regional ≠ individual. A high regional rate does not describe every person in the region; ecological patterns are not individual risks.
No causal claim. The regional pattern co-moves with age structure, remoteness, income, and service access; attribution is M4/M5 work.

  {label: "Daily smoker", t: tSmoke}
]

summary = [
  {series: "Mortality rate (crude)", window: `${mort.start}–${mort.end}`, slope_per_decade: mort.overall.slope_per_decade, verdict: mort.stationarity.verdict, breaks: mort.change_points.join(", ") || "—"},
  {series: "Mortality rate (age-standardised)", window: `${mortAsr.start}–${mortAsr.end}`, slope_per_decade: mortAsr.overall.slope_per_decade, verdict: mortAsr.stationarity.verdict, breaks: mortAsr.change_points.join(", ") || "—"},

  ...survey.map(s => ({series: s.label, window: `${s.t.start}–${s.t.end}`, slope_per_decade: s.t.overall.slope_per_decade, verdict: s.t.stationarity.verdict, breaks: s.t.change_points.join(", ") || "—"}))
]
Inputs.table(summary, {
  columns: ["series", "window", "slope_per_decade", "verdict", "breaks"],
  header: {series: "series", window: "window", slope_per_decade: "slope/decade", verdict: "stationarity", breaks: "regime breaks"}
})






































































































































Several things follow from the table, and they are the report’s core finding:

Almost nothing is stationary. Nearly every series changes over its window; a single summary value would be false to almost all of them. Two — diabetes and having a regular provider — are labelled stationary over their short window, so absence of evidence is reported as such.
Direction differs by measure. The crude mortality rate and life expectancy trend in opposite senses, because crude mortality is not age-adjusted while life expectancy already integrates the age pattern of death; the survey series likewise split, with wellbeing falling while self-reported poor health and mental-health conditions rise.
The change is not one slope. Many series carry a regime break beyond a straight line, several dated to 2020; the breaks are the story, not noise.

title: State of health in BC: a descriptive report
section: Regimes are slope changes, not level shifts
text:
Regimes are slope changes, not level shifts
A regime break can mean two different things: the series steps to a new level, or it keeps its level but changes its rate of movement. The pipeline now separates the two, and for almost every indicator it is the second.

decomp = [
  {series: "Mortality rate (crude)", d: mort},
  {series: "Life expectancy at birth", d: life},
  {series: "Life satisfaction", d: tLifeSat},
  {series: "Sense of belonging", d: tBelong},
  {series: "Anxiety disorder", d: tAnx},
  {series: "Mood disorder", d: tMood},
  {series: "Perceived mental health, fair or poor", d: tMentH},
  {series: "Perceived health, fair or poor", d: tPhyH},
  {series: "Daily smoker", d: tSmoke},
  {series: "High blood pressure", d: tBp},
  {series: "Diabetes", d: tDiab},
  {series: "Has a regular provider", d: tProv}
].map(({series, d}) => ({
  series,
  observed: d.decomposition.observed_change,
  within: d.decomposition.within_regime_change,
  between: d.decomposition.between_regime_change,
  share_between: d.decomposition.observed_change !== 0
    ? Math.abs(d.decomposition.between_regime_change) / (Math.abs(d.decomposition.within_regime_change) + Math.abs(d.decomposition.between_regime_change))
    : 0,
  jumps: d.jumps.map(j => `${j.year}: ${j.jump.toFixed(2)}`).join("; ") || "—"
}))
Inputs.table(decomp, {
  columns: ["series", "observed", "within", "between", "jumps"],
  header: {series: "series", observed: "total change", within: "within-regime", between: "between-regime (jumps)", jumps: "jumps (year: level shift)"},
  width: {jumps: 200}
})
















biggest = decomp.filter(d => d.jumps !== "—").sort((a, b) => Math.abs(b.between) - Math.abs(a.between))
top = biggest[0]
md`The "between-regime" column is nearly zero for all but one series. The
largest level shift anywhere is life expectancy at 2015
(**${life.jumps[0].jump.toFixed(2)}** years), and even there the bulk of the
change is within-regime (${life.decomposition.within_regime_change.toFixed(2)}
of ${life.decomposition.observed_change.toFixed(2)}). For the survey series
the jumps are fractions of a point. So when this report says a series'
"rules change", it means the **slope** changes: the direction and pace of
movement turn, but the series does not lurch discontinuously to a new
level. That is the more common — and more policy-relevant — kind of
nonstationarity.`

Plot.plot({
  title: "Mortality rate, British Columbia (per 1,000 population)",
  x: {label: "Year", tickFormat: "d"},
  y: {grid: true, label: "Deaths per 1,000 population"},
  color: {legend: true},
  marks: [

    Plot.ruleX(mort.change_points, {stroke: "red", strokeDasharray: "4,4"}),
    Plot.ruleX(mortAsr.change_points, {stroke: "steelblue", strokeDasharray: "2,3"}),

md`Over ${mort.start}–${mort.end} the **crude** rate rose by
**${mort.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}** per 1,000 per decade, while the
**age-standardised** rate, which removes the effect of population ageing,
changed by **${mortAsr.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}** — i.e. it *fell*
on net. The crude rise is largely the ageing of the population, not a
worsening of age-specific risk. The age-standardised series is the one that
abstracts from that: it declined from 1991 and its regime turned at
**${mortAsr.change_point}**, after which the decline flattened and
reversed. The pink band marks the COVID-19 period (2020–2024).`






The gap between the two lines is the signature of demographic ageing, and it is exactly why the project reports both and treats the standardised series as the one about risk rather than the one about the age structure. The age breakdown makes the mechanism explicit: the decline is real at every age, but it scales with age (about 9.7 per 1,000 per decade at 90 and over against 0.00 at 30–34), so a rising all-ages crude rate coexists with falling rates at every age. The full breakdown is on the mortality indicator page.

**${life.overall.slope_per_decade.toFixed(2)}** years per decade on average

mortality ranges from **${prem.lowest.value.toFixed(1)}** in
${prem.lowest.region.replace(" Health Service Delivery Area", "")} to
**${prem.highest.value.toFixed(1)}** in
${prem.highest.region.replace(" Health Service Delivery Area", "")} — a
**${prem.ratio.toFixed(1)}×** gap, against a provincial average of about
${prem.mean.toFixed(0)}. Potentially avoidable mortality shows the same
pattern (${avoid.ratio.toFixed(1)}×). The dashed line is the mean across

highest, the Vancouver-metro areas lowest.`






This is a genuine inequality signal, and it is exactly what a provincial-average report hides. Two limits apply. First, the source is three-year averages and covers only two overlapping periods, so it supports this cross-sectional snapshot but not a regional trajectory — the trend machinery is not run on it. Second, the rate confidence intervals overlap between neighbouring regions, so the ordering at the middle of the distribution is not sharp; the roughly 3× gap between the extremes is. No causal claim is made here: the regional pattern co-moves with age structure, remoteness, and service access, which are M4/M5 questions.

title: State of health in BC: a descriptive report
text:
Reading this report

Dates are the point. Every number above belongs to its window; reproducing the pipeline on refreshed data may change the verdicts.
Proxies, several domains. Mortality and life expectancy are mortality-domain proxies; the survey family adds self-reported morbidity, mental health, wellbeing, and access to care. None is the state of health itself, and a self-report is not a diagnosis.
Break detection is not explanation. The dated regimes come from a formal test of departure from a straight line (Truong et al. 2020); the test says where the rule changes, not why. Attribution is M4/M5 work.
Aggregates hide sub-series. A both-sexes series is not a summary of the male and female trajectories; read them separately.
Survey versus administrative. The mortality series are administrative (complete counts), the survey series are samples: the latter carry sampling error, suppression, and a mid-series collection change, so a survey step may be measurement, not change.
